performers: Nanny Larsen-Todsen, soprano; Bayreuth Festival Orchestra; Karl Elmendorff
intro: Isolde looks at Tristan’s body and sees him smiling. Nanny Larsen-Todsen sings her last vision over muted strings, sweeping harp figures and the long-delayed peace of B major.

sections.label: A · Isolde sees Tristan smiling
sections.mNote: Bass clarinet and muted cellos surround the first quiet words

sections.label: B · Harp notes flow beneath the voice
sections.mNote: Harp figures and trembling strings carry the soprano’s long phrases

sections.label: Dev · Isolde hears waves around her

cues.title: A voice above muted cellos
cues.text: “Mild und leise, wie er lächelt” — “Softly and gently, how he smiles.” Isolde’s first words rise above muted, divided cellos. The bass clarinet has its own tender phrase; a clarinet and then the horns join it. The violins wait.
cues.evidence: Wagner’s Act III text, sung by Isolde over Tristan’s body. Breitkopf & Härtel, Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, plate Part. B. 1544, p. 14: bass clarinet, divided muted cellos, subsequent clarinet and horn entries. Own translation. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Isolde sees what others cannot
cues.text: “Seht ihr, Freunde?” — “Do you see, friends?” Isolde asks the people around Tristan’s body to share her vision. She describes his opening eyes, his swelling heart, his breath. The man on the ground is dead.
cues.evidence: Wagner’s libretto, Act III, Isolde’s final monologue; Breitkopf excerpt score, pp. 14–18. Own translation of ‘Seht ihr, Freunde?’ The preceding death of Tristan is described in the Act III synopsis at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde.

cues.title: Harp beneath the long phrases
cues.text: The harp’s figures flow up through trembling strings. High flute notes stretch across the bar while the soprano keeps her own, slower line. The orchestra moves in small, quick notes beneath a voice that still has room to breathe.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 18–22, harp entry and developing arpeggios, divided string tremolos, high flute phrases and sustained vocal writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From Agathe to Isolde
cues.text: Larsen-Todsen begins her stage career in Stockholm in 1906 as Agathe in Weber’s Der Freischütz. She grows into Wagner’s great soprano parts. In 1928 she sings Isolde at Bayreuth and records the role with Karl Elmendorff and the festival orchestra.
cues.evidence: Dr Anton Odelga, biographical note on Preiser LV 174; recording entry for ‘Mild und leise’, Columbia L 2206, 1928, Bayreuth Festival Orchestra, Karl Elmendorff. https://archive.org/download/nanny-larsen-todsen-preiser-lv-174-side-a/Larsen-Todsen%20Preiser%20%282%29.JPG.

cues.title: Waves in words and orchestra
cues.text: Isolde hears sounds swelling around her and wonders whether they are waves of air. The harp sweeps up and down; strings circle through quick figures. Above them, the wind instruments repeat a broad rising phrase, swelling and subsiding while the smaller notes keep going.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 23–25, especially rehearsal Hh on p. 24: ‘mich umwallend, sind es Wellen sanfter Lüfte’, harp arpeggios, continuous string figures and repeated wind phrases with swells.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piccolo above the voice
cues.text: The piccolo and first violins reach high above Isolde. The harp sweeps across its strings, and brass hold the harmony underneath. Her melody moves in long notes through this brilliant company. The orchestra does the running for her.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 27–28, piccolo and high violin writing, wide harp arpeggios, sustained brass chords and Isolde’s long notes at ‘Welt-Atems wehendem All’.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra finishes the sentence
cues.text: Isolde’s last words are “höchste Lust” — “supreme bliss”. The harp keeps moving after she falls silent. The closing music settles into B major, and the last arpeggios give way to a held chord marked pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Wagner’s Act III text, final words of Isolde; own translation. Breitkopf score, pp. 29–30, harp continuation after the vocal release, final B-major chord, pp and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The wind phrases rise over circling strings
transitions.from: B · Harp notes flow beneath the voice
transitions.to: Dev · Isolde hears waves around her
transitions.how: Long bass notes support repeated rising phrases in the woodwind. Trumpets and trombones sustain the harmony, while the harp sweeps up and down and the strings keep circling in quick notes. Each broad wind phrase swells, then withdraws; Isolde’s line continues through these successive waves.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 23–25, rehearsal Hh: long bass notes, sustained brass, repeated woodwind phrases, string figures and harp arpeggios.

transitions.title: The voice leaves the harp moving
transitions.to: Coda · The last words and B major
transitions.how: The high violin figures turn downwards and the brass recede. Harp arpeggios continue beneath Isolde’s last phrase, then beneath the orchestra alone. A sustained bass and increasingly quiet wind chords lead towards B major. The harp finally stops running; the last chord is held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 29–30: descending violin figures, diminishing brass, harp continuation, final B-major cadence and fermata. The preserved section boundary marks the approach to this closing passage.

source.title: Wagner: Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, with vocal part — Breitkopf & Härtel
source.locator: Printed pp. 14–30; broad score-proportion landmarks, not bar-synchronised entrances.

timeline.note: Opening span, p. 14: low tremolando strings support Isolde; bass clarinet and trombones enter softly.
Approximate first expansion, pp. 15–17: brighter woodwind and harp join the string-and-voice texture.
Approximate middle span: woodwind responses and active inner strings accompany the continuing vocal line.
Broad accumulating span, pp. 24–27: harp, woodwind and strings remain active as brass reinforces the rises.
Late climactic region, pp. 27–28; the timestamp marks the strongest audio crest, not each instrumental entrance.

Final orchestral cadence, p. 30. The voice has finished; quiet wind and string lines settle into the final chords. Cor anglais and timpani contribute within this closing region, not continuously throughout it.

composer.epithet: He hid the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth and taught it to remember everything his characters wanted to forget.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no success worth mentioning. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons calling across the strings’ storm. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to persuade somebody to stage his music.

He had grown up inside the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies supplied the sounds; Theodor Weinlig supplied counterpoint lessons in 1831. Jobs followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen remained unperformed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, collapsed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
